warmup.q: On a day when nothing was baked, cookies is empty. What does cookies.reduce { a, b -> if (a.grams >= b.grams) a else b } do?
options: Throws UnsupportedOperationException: Empty collection can't be reduced.
Doesn't compile, because reduce needs a starting value
warmup.why: reduce starts from the first element, and an empty list has none, so Kotlin throws. Java's Stream.reduce without a starting value returns Optional.empty, which is why the third option is tempting. In Kotlin you choose explicitly: reduceOrNull, maxByOrNull, or fold with a starting value. The section on fold lines them all up.

opening:
Picture a baking day. Two trays of cookies come out of the oven. Most are golden, one is burnt, one is still raw in the middle, and someone has already taken a bite of another. You want to know a few things: how much good cookie there is, by flavor, which ones to throw away, and which golden one is the biggest.

Nobody does that by saying "for each cookie, if it's golden, add it to this pile, and if it's burnt...". You take out the burnt ones, sort the rest by flavor, and weigh each pile. Each job is one step.

Code usually says "for each cookie" anyway. One loop builds four results at once, every line changes one of them, and it works fine until a day when nothing was baked. The last lesson, on higher-order functions, wrote functions that take functions. Kotlin's collection library is a set of them, ready-made.

In this lesson, we'll watch a report loop fail on an empty day, then rebuild it from map, filter, fold and their friends, with the trap each one hides. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with two trays of cookies and a loop that built four results at once, then threw on a day when nothing was baked. Each result became one chain: filter and sumOf for the golden grams, groupBy for flavors in first-seen order, maxByOrNull for a largest that can be nothing, and fold for the jar, the loop with its var tucked inside.

Search your code for .first(), .reduce { and associateBy. Ask of each one: what happens on an empty day, or when a tray is written down twice?

Next, we'll stop a chain from building a new list at every step. What changes when one cookie at a time travels the whole pipeline?

sections.h: A baking-day report written as one loop, and the two bugs it hides
sections.html:
Here is the end-of-day report the way most of us first write it. A Cookie has an id, a flavor, its weight in grams from the kitchen scale, a status (GOLDEN, RAW or BURNT) and nibbledGrams, which is null unless someone took a bite. One pass over the cookies builds four results:

Java
int golden = 0;
Map<String, Integer> net = new LinkedHashMap<>();
List<String> burnt = new ArrayList<>();
Cookie largest = cookies.get(0);
for (Cookie c : cookies) {
    switch (c.status()) {
        case GOLDEN -> {
            golden += c.grams();
            net.merge(c.flavor(), c.grams() - biteOf(c), Integer::sum);
            if (c.grams() > largest.grams()) largest = c;
        }
        case BURNT -> burnt.add(c.id());
        case RAW -> { }
    }
}
Kotlin
var golden = 0
val net = LinkedHashMap<String, Int>()
val burnt = ArrayList<String>()
var largest = cookies.first()
for (c in cookies) {
    when (c.status) {
        Status.GOLDEN -> {
            golden += c.grams
            net[c.flavor] = (net[c.flavor] ?: 0) + c.grams - (c.nibbledGrams ?: 0)
            if (c.grams > largest.grams) largest = c
        }
        Status.BURNT -> burnt.add(c.id)
        Status.RAW -> {}
    }
}

It works on a normal day. It's also hard to read, for a reason you can name: four results are being built at the same time, interleaved, and every line changes one of them. To check how largest is worked out, you have to read the whole loop, because any line might touch it.

And it has two bugs that a normal day never shows. On a day with no cookies, cookies.first() throws NoSuchElementException: List is empty. (Java's get(0) throws an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException). And say the first cookie of the day is a raw one of 99 g. largest starts there, no golden cookie beats it, and the report proudly names a cookie that is still dough.

Here is the same report written with collection operations. Each one is a function from the standard library that takes a lambda and does one job over the whole list:

Java
List<Cookie> goldenCookies = cookies.stream().filter(c -> c.status() == GOLDEN).toList();
int golden = goldenCookies.stream().mapToInt(Cookie::grams).sum();
Map<String, Integer> net = goldenCookies.stream().collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
        Cookie::flavor, LinkedHashMap::new, Collectors.summingInt(c -> c.grams() - biteOf(c))));
List<String> burnt = cookies.stream().filter(c -> c.status() == BURNT).map(Cookie::id).toList();
Optional<Cookie> largest = goldenCookies.stream().max(Comparator.comparingInt(Cookie::grams));
Kotlin
val goldenCookies = cookies.filter { it.status == Status.GOLDEN }
val golden = goldenCookies.sumOf { it.grams }
val net = goldenCookies.groupBy { it.flavor }
    .mapValues { (_, cs) -> cs.sumOf { it.grams - (it.nibbledGrams ?: 0) } }
val burnt = cookies.filter { it.status == Status.BURNT }.map { it.id }
val largest = goldenCookies.maxByOrNull { it.grams }

Each result is one val, computed from the list, and each line says what it computes rather than how to walk the list. The ReportLoop demo prints both versions:

chain: golden=125 net={oat=85, chocolate=30} burnt=[c4] largest=c3
loop:  golden=125 net={oat=85, chocolate=30} burnt=[c4] largest=c3

Same answers on a normal day. Both bugs are gone without anyone hunting for them: maxByOrNull only ever sees golden cookies and returns null for an empty list, and nothing assumes there is a first element.

Give each result its own chain. A loop that fills four piles at once makes every line a suspect.

The rest of this lesson takes those operations one at a time, with the trap that comes with each.

try.title: Break the loop with an empty day
steps: Run ReportLoop (or ReportLoopJava). Check that the loop and the chain agree on the sample day.
Run it again with -Pargs=empty added. Predict first: which version survives a day with no cookies?

Put a raw cookie of 99 g at the front of the sample day, Cookie("c0", "oat", 99, Status.RAW) in sampleDay in SampleDay.kt (Java: new Cookie("c0", "oat", 99, Status.RAW, null) in DAY), and run once more. Compare the two largest values.

code.title: ReportLoop.kt
code.html: package workbench.functional.l04.demo // Cookie, Status and sampleDay are in SampleDay.kt, next to this file. // The loop: four results built at once, and every line changes one of them. fun reportLoop(cookies: List<Cookie>): String { var golden = 0 val net = LinkedHashMap<String, Int>() val burnt = ArrayList<String>() var largest = cookies.first() for (c in cookies) { when (c.status) { Status.GOLDEN -> { golden += c.grams net[c.flavor] = (net[c.flavor] ?: 0) + c.grams - (c.nibbledGrams ?: 0) if (c.grams > largest.grams) largest = c } Status.BURNT -> burnt.add(c.id) Status.RAW -> {} } } return "golden=$golden net=$net burnt=$burnt largest=${largest.id}" } // The same report: one val per result, each computed from the list. fun reportChain(cookies: List<Cookie>): String { val goldenCookies = cookies.filter { it.status == Status.GOLDEN } val golden = goldenCookies.sumOf { it.grams } val net = goldenCookies.groupBy { it.flavor } .mapValues { (_, cs) -> cs.sumOf { it.grams - (it.nibbledGrams ?: 0) } } val burnt = cookies.filter { it.status == Status.BURNT }.map { it.id } val largest = goldenCookies.maxByOrNull { it.grams } return "golden=$golden net=$net burnt=$burnt largest=${largest?.id}" } fun main(args: Array<String>) { val cookies = if (args.firstOrNull() == "empty") emptyList() else sampleDay println("chain: ${reportChain(cookies)}") try { println("loop: ${reportLoop(cookies)}") } catch (e: NoSuchElementException) { println("loop: threw $e") } }

try.expect: On the sample day both print golden=125 net={oat=85, chocolate=30} burnt=[c4] largest=c3. On the empty day the chain prints zeros, an empty map and largest=null, and the loop throws java.util.NoSuchElementException: List is empty. (Java: ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: Index 0 out of bounds for length 0). With the big raw cookie first, the loop reports that raw cookie as the largest; the chain still says c3.

sections.h: One job per step: map, filter, mapNotNull and flatMap
sections.html:
Each collection operation does one job and returns a new collection, so you read a chain top to bottom, one job per line. In the kitchen: weigh every cookie, set aside the burnt ones, tip both trays onto one rack.

  • map transforms every element: cookies.map { it.grams } gives one weight per cookie, in the same order.
  • filter keeps the elements that pass a test: cookies.filter { it.status == GOLDEN }.
  • mapNotNull transforms and drops the nulls in one step. cookies.mapNotNull { it.nibbledGrams } gives just the bites, [10] on the sample day. It replaces map { ... }.filterNotNull() and builds one list instead of two.
  • flatMap turns each element into a list and joins the lists: trays.flatMap { it.cookies } turns a day of trays into one list of cookies.

Then come the operations that boil a list down to one answer: sumOf, count { }, any { }, all { }, none { }, first { } and maxByOrNull { }. Several of them take a predicate, a function that answers true or false. Those stop at the first element that decides the answer, so any stops at its first match.

Java has the same operations on streams. A stream is Java's pipeline object: you make one from a collection with .stream(), add steps, and finish with an operation such as toList() or sum(). Side by side:

Java
List<Integer> bites = cookies.stream()
        .map(Cookie::nibbledGrams)
        .filter(Objects::nonNull)
        .toList();                                          // [10]
List<String> ids = trays.stream()
        .flatMap(t -> t.cookies().stream())
        .map(Cookie::id)
        .toList();
boolean anyBig = cookies.stream().anyMatch(c -> c.grams() > 75);
Kotlin
val bites = cookies.mapNotNull { it.nibbledGrams }        // [10]
val ids = trays.flatMap { it.cookies }.map { it.id }
val anyBig = cookies.any { it.grams > 75 }

The difference that matters isn't the syntax. A Java stream is lazy: nothing runs until the last operation, and then each element travels through the whole pipeline. Kotlin's operations on a List are eager: filter runs over the whole list and returns a new ArrayList, then map runs over that one and returns another. Every step builds a full list in between.

As the last lesson showed, the lambdas cost nothing, because these functions are inline. The lists are the cost. For a day of a few hundred cookies that's nothing. For a million rows and five steps it starts to matter, and the next lesson's sequences are the fix.

This is also where the tray picture breaks. In a kitchen, cookies move along one at a time: you weigh one and pass it on. Kotlin's list operations finish the whole tray before the next step starts, onto a fresh tray each time.

One rule keeps a chain honest: no side effects inside it. A map that also writes to a file, or a filter that bumps a counter, brings back exactly the hidden state that lesson 1 removed. Effects go at the end, in a forEach, or better, in the shell from lesson 1.

A chain computes and the shell acts. Keep side effects out of map and filter.

Most of these operations are named versions of one general loop. The next section gives it its name.

try.expect: map gives all five weights, [45, 90, 50, 80, 30], filter gives [c1, c3, c5], mapNotNull gives [10], flatMap gives the five ids in tray order, sumOf 295, count 3, any / all true / true, and partition [c1, c3, c5] / [c2, c4]. Plain map gives [null, null, 10, null, null], a List<Int?>, and .sum() on it fails with none of the following candidates is applicable, because sum only exists for lists of non-null numbers. Kotlin's map returns a fresh java.util.ArrayList; Java's toList() returns an unmodifiable ImmutableCollections$ListN.

sections.h: The loop you were writing is a fold
sections.html:
Every loop that builds one result has the same two parts: a starting value, and a step that combines the result so far with the next element. fold is that loop with both parts passed in.

Our example is the cookie jar. It already holds 200 g. At the end of the day each golden cookie goes in, minus any bite, and the raw and burnt ones stay out:

Java
int jar = cookies.stream().reduce(200,
        (acc, c) -> c.status() == GOLDEN ? acc + c.grams() - biteOf(c) : acc,
        Integer::sum);                  // the third argument only matters for parallel streams
Kotlin
val jar = cookies.fold(200) { jar, c ->
    when (c.status) {
        Status.GOLDEN -> jar + c.grams - (c.nibbledGrams ?: 0)
        Status.RAW, Status.BURNT -> jar
    }
}

The value carried from one step to the next is the accumulator, jar here. Picture yourself at the jar with the kitchen scale. You carry one number, the jar's weight, past each cookie in turn, and each cookie either changes it or doesn't. The figure below walks it from 200 g to 315 g.

The standard library's fold is the loop you'd write by hand: var accumulator = initial; for (element in this) accumulator = operation(accumulator, element); return accumulator. It's inline, so your lambda is pasted into that loop. The var still exists, but it lives inside fold where nothing else can touch it, and your own code has only vals.

sumOf, count, maxByOrNull and joinToString are all special cases of fold, already written and named. Prefer them when they fit, because sumOf { it.grams } says more than fold(0) { acc, c -> acc + c.grams }. Reach for fold when the step needs a when, as the jar does, or when the accumulator is something richer than a number.

reduce looks like fold without the starting value. It uses the first element as the start instead, and that's the trap: an empty list has no first element. Here's what Kotlin 2.4.21 does with an empty list of weights, from the EmptyTraps demo:

fold(0) { a, b -> a + b }        0
sum()                            0
reduceOrNull { a, b -> a + b }   null
reduce { a, b -> a + b }         throws java.lang.UnsupportedOperationException: Empty collection can't be reduced.
first()                          throws java.util.NoSuchElementException: List is empty.
firstOrNull()                    null
maxOf { it }                     throws java.util.NoSuchElementException
maxOrNull()                      null

Java chose differently. Stream.reduce without a starting value returns an Optional, a box that may be empty, so the type makes you handle the empty case. Kotlin gives you two names instead, a throwing one and an OrNull one.

An empty list is a normal day. Use fold, sumOf or an OrNull function when the input can be empty.

Keep reduce and first() for the places where an empty list is a bug you want to hear about loudly.

Folding gives one answer. Reports usually want an answer per flavor or per tray, and that means a map.

Java's answer to "no elements" is mostly Optional. */ public class EmptyTrapsJava { // Runs one expression and prints its value, or the exception it threw. static void attempt(String label, Supplier<Object> block) { String result; try { result = String.valueOf(block.get()); } catch (RuntimeException e) { result = "throws " + e; } System.out.printf("%-40s %s%n", label, result); } public static void main(String[] args) { List<Integer> none = List.of(); // a day when nothing was baked attempt("reduce(0, Integer::sum)", () -> none.stream().reduce(0, Integer::sum)); attempt("mapToInt(x -> x).sum()", () -> none.stream().mapToInt(x -> x).sum()); attempt("reduce(Integer::sum)", () -> none.stream().reduce(Integer::sum)); attempt("findFirst()", () -> none.stream().findFirst()); attempt("findFirst().orElseThrow()", () -> none.stream().findFirst().orElseThrow()); attempt("get(0)", () -> none.get(0)); attempt("max(Integer::compare)", () -> none.stream().max(Integer::compare)); } }

try.expect: On the empty list, fold and sum give 0; reduceOrNull, firstOrNull and maxOrNull give null; reduce, first() and maxOf throw, with the messages in the table above. The Java version prints 0 for both sums and Optional.empty for reduce without a starting value, for findFirst() and for max. It throws NoSuchElementException: No value present from orElseThrow() and ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException from get(0). With two weights every line returns a value: 95 for the folds, sums and reduces, 45 for first(), 50 for the max.

sections.h: From a list to a map: groupBy, associateBy and partition
sections.html:
Reports are mostly maps: grams per flavor, cookies by id, counts per status. A map is a lookup table from keys to values. Three operations build one from a list, and each has a behaviour worth knowing before it surprises you.

groupBy puts every element into a list under its key, like sorting cookies into jars by flavor:

Java
Map<String, List<String>> byFlavor = cookies.stream().collect(
        Collectors.groupingBy(Cookie::flavor, Collectors.mapping(Cookie::id, Collectors.toList())));
// {oat=[c1, c3], ginger=[c4], chocolate=[c2, c5]}   a HashMap: no order promised
Kotlin
val byFlavor = cookies.groupBy({ it.flavor }, { it.id })
// {oat=[c1, c3], chocolate=[c2, c5], ginger=[c4]}   a LinkedHashMap: first-seen order

Kotlin's groupBy returns a LinkedHashMap, a map that remembers the order its keys arrived in. Its documentation promises that keys keep the order in which they were first seen. Java's groupingBy promises nothing about the map it returns. On JDK 21 it was a plain HashMap, which keeps keys in an order of its own, and it put ginger before chocolate.

If a report must list flavors in the order they came out of the oven, Kotlin does that for you, and in Java you pass LinkedHashMap::new. When you only need a number per group, groupingBy { it.flavor }.eachCount() computes it in one pass. So does groupingBy { it.flavor }.fold(0) { acc, c -> acc + c.grams }, and neither builds a list for each group.

associateBy builds a map with one element per key. Here the two languages part ways:

Java
Map<String, String> oneEach = cookies.stream()
        .collect(Collectors.toMap(Cookie::flavor, Cookie::id));
// throws IllegalStateException: Duplicate key oat (attempted merging values c1 and c3)
Kotlin
val oneEach = cookies.associateBy({ it.flavor }, { it.id })
// {oat=c3, chocolate=c5, ginger=c4}   c1 and c2 are gone, without a word

When two elements share a key, associateBy keeps the last one and says nothing. Java's toMap throws. For cookies keyed by an id that should be unique, Java's behaviour is the one you want.

Say someone writes the second tray down twice. The same cookies arrive twice, associateBy quietly keeps one copy of each, and nobody hears about the mistake. So check before you index. cookies.groupingBy { it.id }.eachCount().filterValues { it > 1 } lists every repeated id, and the lab's indexById refuses a day that has any.

associateBy keeps the last value for a repeated key, without a word. Check for repeats first.

partition splits a list in two by a predicate, and destructuring (unpacking a pair into two vals) makes it read well: val (golden, rest) = cookies.partition { it.status == GOLDEN }. Java's version is Collectors.partitioningBy, which returns a Map<Boolean, List<Cookie>>.

With these, the report from the first section is complete, and the lab builds it. Every one of these operations shares the limit from the second section, though: each step builds a whole new list or map before the next one starts.

try.title: Find the line that loses data
steps: Run DuplicateKeys (or DuplicateKeysJava). Compare the key order of Kotlin's groupBy with Java's groupingBy.
Find the line that loses data without telling you. Which cookies are missing from it?

In the Java version, give toMap a third argument, (a, b) -> b, and run. In the Kotlin version, add a line that prints the repeated flavors: groupingBy { it.flavor }.eachCount().filterValues { it > 1 }.keys.

code.title: DuplicateKeys.kt
code.html: package workbench.functional.l04.demo // Cookie, Status and sampleDay are in SampleDay.kt, next to this file. fun main() { val byFlavor = sampleDay.groupBy({ it.flavor }, { it.id }) println("groupBy: $byFlavor") println("map class: ${byFlavor.javaClass.name}") // One value per key. oat and chocolate each have two cookies. Which ones survive? println("associateBy: ${sampleDay.associateBy({ it.flavor }, { it.id })}") // Counting per key in one pass, with no list per group. println("eachCount: ${sampleDay.groupingBy { it.flavor }.eachCount()}") }

alt.title: DuplicateKeysJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.functional.l04.demo; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; import java.util.stream.Collectors; /** Java twin of DuplicateKeys.kt. Same data, different defaults: no key order, and toMap throws. */ public class DuplicateKeysJava { enum Status { GOLDEN, RAW, BURNT } record Cookie(String id, String flavor, int grams, Status status, Integer nibbledGrams) {} static final List<Cookie> DAY = List.of( new Cookie("c1", "oat", 45, Status.GOLDEN, null), new Cookie("c2", "chocolate", 90, Status.RAW, null), new Cookie("c3", "oat", 50, Status.GOLDEN, 10), new Cookie("c4", "ginger", 80, Status.BURNT, null), new Cookie("c5", "chocolate", 30, Status.GOLDEN, null)); public static void main(String[] args) { Map<String, List<String>> byFlavor = DAY.stream().collect( Collectors.groupingBy(Cookie::flavor, Collectors.mapping(Cookie::id, Collectors.toList()))); System.out.println("groupingBy: " + byFlavor); System.out.println("map class: " + byFlavor.getClass().getName()); // One value per key. oat and chocolate each have two cookies. try { System.out.println("toMap: " + DAY.stream().collect(Collectors.toMap(Cookie::flavor, Cookie::id))); } catch (IllegalStateException e) { System.out.println("toMap: threw " + e); } // Counting per key. System.out.println("counting: " + DAY.stream().collect( Collectors.groupingBy(Cookie::flavor, Collectors.counting()))); } }

try.expect: Kotlin prints oat, chocolate, ginger in first-seen order, from a java.util.LinkedHashMap. Java's groupingBy prints oat, ginger, chocolate, from a java.util.HashMap. associateBy keeps c3, c5 and c4: c1 and c2 vanished silently. Java's plain toMap throws IllegalStateException: Duplicate key oat (attempted merging values c1 and c3); with (a, b) -> b it keeps the last value and behaves exactly like associateBy. The repeated flavors are [oat, chocolate].

compare.title: The baking-day report with streams and with Kotlin collection functions

java.title: Report.java
java.html: static BakeReport report(List<Tray> trays) { List<Cookie> cookies = trays.stream().flatMap(t -> t.cookies().stream()).toList(); Map<String, Cookie> byId = cookies.stream() .collect(Collectors.toMap(Cookie::id, c -> c)); // throws on a repeated id List<Cookie> golden = cookies.stream().filter(c -> c.status() == GOLDEN).toList(); return new BakeReport( cookies.size(), golden.stream().mapToInt(Cookie::grams).sum(), cookies.stream().map(Cookie::nibbledGrams).filter(Objects::nonNull) .mapToInt(Integer::intValue).sum(), golden.stream().collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Cookie::flavor, LinkedHashMap::new, // or no order is promised Collectors.summingInt(c -> c.grams() - biteOf(c)))), cookies.stream().filter(c -> c.status() == BURNT).map(Cookie::id).toList(), golden.stream().max(Comparator.comparingInt(Cookie::grams))); // Optional<Cookie> }

kotlin.title: Report.kt
kotlin.html: fun report(trays: List<Tray>): BakeReport { val cookies = trays.flatMap { it.cookies } val repeated = cookies.groupingBy { it.id }.eachCount().filterValues { it > 1 }.keys require(repeated.isEmpty()) { "duplicate cookie ids: ${repeated.joinToString()}" } // associateBy would not val golden = cookies.filter { it.status == GOLDEN } return BakeReport( cookieCount = cookies.size, goldenGrams = golden.sumOf { it.grams }, nibbledGrams = cookies.mapNotNull { it.nibbledGrams }.sum(), netByFlavor = golden.groupBy { it.flavor } // first-seen order .mapValues { (_, cs) -> cs.sumOf { it.grams - (it.nibbledGrams ?: 0) } }, burntIds = cookies.filter { it.status == BURNT }.map { it.id }, largestGolden = golden.maxByOrNull { it.grams }, // Cookie?, null when none ) }

compare.note: The vocabulary is nearly the same, and the defaults are not. Java streams are lazy and single-use and finish with a collector; Kotlin's list functions are eager, return ordinary lists and maps, and can be called again on the same list. Java says "maybe nothing" with Optional, Kotlin with a nullable type and the OrNull functions. Java's groupingBy promises no key order unless you pass a map factory, while Kotlin's groupBy keeps first-seen order. And the duplicate-key defaults are opposite: Java's toMap throws, Kotlin's associateBy keeps the last value, so in Kotlin the duplicate check is your job.

worked.title: Rewrite a nested-loop match of reviews to recipes

steps.say: A recipe site matches each review to the recipe it belongs to, by recipeId. Here is a direct translation of two nested loops into a chain. Before reading on, estimate how many comparisons it makes for 10,000 recipes and 2,000 reviews.
steps.code: val matched = recipes.flatMap { r -> reviews.filter { it.recipeId == r.id }.map { rv -> r to rv } }

alt.html: List<Map.Entry<Recipe, Review>> matched = recipes.stream() .flatMap(r -> reviews.stream() .filter(rv -> rv.recipeId().equals(r.id())) .map(rv -> Map.entry(r, rv))) .toList();

steps.say: 1. Count the work. The inner filter runs over every review for every recipe: 10,000 x 2,000 = 20 million comparisons, plus one small list per recipe. A chain is no faster than the loop it replaced; it only reads better. 2. Index once instead: build a map from id to recipe, then look each review up. (?.let runs its lambda only when the lookup found something; lesson 6 covers it.)
steps.code: val recipesById = recipes.associateBy { it.id } // 1. one pass: 10,000 entries val matched = reviews.mapNotNull { rv -> // 2. one pass: 2,000 lookups recipesById[rv.recipeId]?.let { r -> r to rv } }

alt.html: Map<String, Recipe> recipesById = recipes.stream() .collect(Collectors.toMap(Recipe::id, r -> r)); // 1. one pass; throws on a repeated id List<Map.Entry<Recipe, Review>> matched = reviews.stream() // 2. one lookup per review .filter(rv -> recipesById.containsKey(rv.recipeId())) .map(rv -> Map.entry(recipesById.get(rv.recipeId()), rv)) .toList();

steps.say: 1. Decide what duplicates and orphans mean. associateBy keeps the last recipe for a repeated id, so check for repeats first, as the lab does. And mapNotNull silently drops reviews whose recipe isn't in the list, say because it was deleted. Self-check: is dropping them right? (Usually not. An orphan review is worth reporting, so split them out with partition and keep both lists.)
steps.code: val (known, orphans) = reviews.partition { it.recipeId in recipesById } val matched = known.map { rv -> recipesById.getValue(rv.recipeId) to rv } // orphans goes into the report instead of disappearing

alt.html: Map<Boolean, List<Review>> split = reviews.stream() .collect(Collectors.partitioningBy(rv -> recipesById.containsKey(rv.recipeId()))); List<Review> orphans = split.get(false); // goes into the report instead of disappearing List<Map.Entry<Recipe, Review>> matched = split.get(true).stream() .map(rv -> Map.entry(recipesById.get(rv.recipeId()), rv)) .toList();

lab.title: Rewrite the baking-day report without loops
steps: Run the tests. All twelve fail with NotImplementedError. Open Cookies.kt and read bakeReportLoop, the version you are replacing. Don't edit it. A Tray is one tray out of the oven, and a baking day is a list of trays.
In Report.kt, write allCookies, goldenGrams, nibbledGrams and burntIds. Each is one chain, and each TODO names the operations.
Write netByFlavor with groupBy and mapValues, and largestGolden with maxByOrNull. Read the test names first: key order and the null case both count.
Write jarGrams with fold and a when expression inside the lambda.
Write indexById: find repeated ids with groupingBy { it.id }.eachCount(), throw with require if there are any, then associateBy.

Write bakeReport from the functions above, calling indexById first. Run the tests until all twelve pass. Then look at the empty-day and largest-golden tests and work out how bakeReportLoop would fail each one.
hints: mapValues { (_, cs) -> cs.sumOf { ... } } destructures each map entry; _ skips the key you don't need.
require(condition) { message } throws IllegalArgumentException(message) when the condition is false. joinToString() joins with ", " by default.
nibbledGrams ?: 0 turns a missing bite into zero, so the subtraction works for every golden cookie.
lab.done: All twelve tests in BakeReportTest pass, and Report.kt has no for and no var.

drill.title: Write the report chain from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Given cookies: List<Cookie> with id, flavor, grams and status, write from memory: the golden total; the golden total per flavor in first-seen order; the number of burnt cookies; the heaviest golden cookie, or nothing; and a map from id to cookie that refuses repeated ids. Then write the same five results with Java streams. Which Java line needs an extra argument to keep the flavor order?

answer.html: val golden = cookies.filter { it.status == Status.GOLDEN } val total = golden.sumOf { it.grams } val perFlavor = golden.groupBy { it.flavor }.mapValues { (_, cs) -> cs.sumOf { it.grams } } val burntCount = cookies.count { it.status == Status.BURNT } val heaviest = golden.maxByOrNull { it.grams } // null when nothing came out golden val repeated = cookies.groupingBy { it.id }.eachCount().filterValues { it > 1 }.keys require(repeated.isEmpty()) { "duplicate cookie ids: ${repeated.joinToString()}" } val byId = cookies.associateBy { it.id }

alt.html: List<Cookie> golden = cookies.stream().filter(c -> c.status() == Status.GOLDEN).toList(); int total = golden.stream().mapToInt(Cookie::grams).sum(); Map<String, Integer> perFlavor = golden.stream().collect(Collectors.groupingBy( Cookie::flavor, LinkedHashMap::new, // the extra argument: keeps the order Collectors.summingInt(Cookie::grams))); long burntCount = cookies.stream().filter(c -> c.status() == Status.BURNT).count(); Optional<Cookie> heaviest = golden.stream().max(Comparator.comparingInt(Cookie::grams)); Map<String, Cookie> byId = cookies.stream() .collect(Collectors.toMap(Cookie::id, c -> c)); // throws on a repeated id

recap: map, filter, mapNotNull and flatMap each do one job and return a new list. Read a chain top to bottom, one job per line.
fold(initial) { acc, x -> ... } is the general loop with its var hidden inside. sumOf, count and maxByOrNull are named special cases; prefer them when they fit.

On an empty list, reduce throws UnsupportedOperationException: Empty collection can't be reduced. and first() throws NoSuchElementException: List is empty. Use fold, sumOf or the OrNull functions when input can be empty.
groupBy keeps first-seen key order in a LinkedHashMap. Java's groupingBy promises no order unless you pass LinkedHashMap::new.
associateBy silently keeps the last element for a repeated key, where Java's toMap throws. When keys should be unique, check for repeats first.
The limit: Kotlin's operations on a List are eager. Each step builds a whole new ArrayList; the lambdas are free because the functions are inline, but the lists in between are not.

explain.prompt: A teammate who likes loops asks why the chain version of the baking-day report fixed two bugs nobody was hunting for, and what the chain costs that the loop doesn't. Explain it in your own words.
explain.answer: The loop built four results at once with mutable variables, so each one depended on details spread over the whole loop. largest started from cookies.first(), which crashes on an empty day and, on a normal day, starts from whatever cookie came first, even a raw one. In the chain, each result is computed on its own from the list. largest is maxByOrNull over the golden cookies only, so it can't pick a raw one and returns null when there are none, and no line assumes there is a first element. The cost is allocation: Kotlin's list operations are eager, so each filter or map builds a whole new list, where the loop made one pass and built nothing extra. The lambdas themselves are free because the functions are inline. For a few hundred cookies that cost doesn't matter; for millions of rows I'd fuse steps or use a sequence.

deeper.html:
A few more operations earn a place in collection code.

runningFold (also called scan) is fold that keeps every value along the way, which is exactly a running total. Over the weights [45, 90, 50, 80, 30], runningFold(0) { acc, x -> acc + x } gives [0, 45, 135, 185, 265, 295]: one more element than the input, because it includes the starting value. runningReduce leaves the starting value out.

Java
// JDK 21 streams have no running fold; a loop is the plain answer.
List<Integer> totals = new ArrayList<>(List.of(0));
for (int x : grams) totals.add(totals.get(totals.size() - 1) + x);
// JDK 24 added java.util.stream.Gatherers, with scan(...) and windowFixed(...) as intermediate operations.
Kotlin
val totals = grams.runningFold(0) { acc, x -> acc + x }   // [0, 45, 135, 185, 265, 295]
val firstOver200 = totals.indexOfFirst { it > 200 }        // 4: the tray passes 200 g after the fourth cookie

chunked(12) splits cookies into boxes of twelve, and the last box may hold fewer: listOf(1, 2, 3, 4, 5).chunked(2) is [[1, 2], [3, 4], [5]]. windowed(7) gives sliding windows, for a seven-day average of how much you baked. zip pairs two lists element by element and quietly stops at the shorter one, so zipping 10 planned bakes with 9 actual ones loses the 10th without a word: compare the sizes first.

One caution from the other direction. Kotlin's forEach is inline, so a return inside its lambda returns from the enclosing function and skips every remaining element. Java developers expect continue-like behaviour from Stream.forEach. Use return@forEach to skip one element, or better, express the skip with filter.
